answer:
The best chain is QB7-QB12-QB11, with QB12 in the middle. I took the numbers from garnet's current default calibration set, f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade. The default CZ gate there is slepian_crf. All 28 CZ pairs had an IRB fidelity. The QB7-QB12 CZ scored 0.998016 and the QB12-QB11 CZ scored 0.998693. Their product is 0.996712, which is the highest of every connected 3-qubit chain. The next best was QB12-QB11-QB16 at 0.994689.

I then built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit from garnet's native gates. A quarter turn put QB12 into an equal mix of 0 and 1. Two CNOTs then copied that onto QB7 and QB11. Each CNOT was made from a CZ with single-qubit rotations around it. The circuit used exactly 2 CZ gates, one on QB12-QB7 and one on QB12-QB11. It measured all 3 qubits. I simulated the same gates without noise. The ideal result is 50% 000 and 50% 111.

I ran it on garnet:mock with 200 shots as job 01a160a7-12dc-7783-ab97-480b4db65023. The job completed. The server's copy of the circuit showed 2 CZ gates on those two pairs and measurements on QB7, QB12 and QB11. The counts in order QB7, QB12, QB11 were 000: 46, 001: 49, 110: 51 and 111: 54. The mock backend returns random-looking counts that do not follow the circuit. So these counts check that the job and circuit are valid. They do not show entanglement. On the real garnet, a good GHZ run would show almost only 000 and 111. That would mean the three qubits share one state and always agree when measured. The mock job cost 0 credits.

The idea behind picking the chain is this: every CZ gate adds a small error. The chance that both gates work is about the product of their fidelities. Picking the pair of links with the highest product gives the GHZ state its best chance on real hardware.
